en: To warn or scold someone firmly but mildly
hook: ADMONISH: ADD a MONITOR'S warning.
story: When the teacher caught Rafi texting during class, she didn't shout. She simply admonished him: 'Rafi, phones away, or next time it's mine until Friday.' To admonish is to warn or reprimand firmly, but without anger or severe punishment. Parents admonish children; doctors admonish patients who skip their medicine.

en: Concerned with beauty or the appreciation of beauty
hook: AESTHETIC: think 'A STYLISH thing', all about beauty.
story: Nadia rearranged her study room: fairy lights, a small plant, neatly lined books, and a pastel wall. 'It's more aesthetic now,' she said. Aesthetic relates to beauty and artistic taste. Architects consider both function and aesthetics. Don't confuse it with ascetic, which means rejecting pleasure.

en: Behavior or speech that is artificial and meant to impress
hook: AFFECTATION: a FAKE act put on to impress.
story: After six months in London, Tanvir returned to Dhaka speaking with a fake British accent and saying 'brilliant' and 'cheers' in every sentence. His friends rolled their eyes at the affectation. An affectation is an artificial way of behaving, designed to impress others. It isn't genuine; it's a pose.

en: To make pain, suffering, or a problem less severe
hook: ALLEVIATE: to LEVITATE the weight; making the burden lighter.
story: A cold towel and two tablets alleviated Sara's fever within an hour. The illness wasn't cured, but she felt much better. To alleviate is to make suffering easier to bear. A new flyover alleviates traffic congestion; free school meals alleviate hunger. Synonyms: ease, relieve, mitigate.

en: Similar or comparable in some way
hook: ANALOGOUS: makes an ANALOGY possible.
story: The teacher explained: 'The heart is analogous to a water pump. Both push liquid through pipes.' Suddenly the biology lesson made sense. Analogous means comparable, similar in certain ways that allow a useful comparison. GRE analogies depend on spotting analogous relationships.

en: To support or strengthen
hook: BOLSTER: a BOLSTER is a long pillow that props you up.
story: Arif's research paper had a bold claim, so he bolstered it with data from three countries, two expert interviews, and twenty charts. Now his argument stood strong. To bolster is to support or reinforce, like a firm pillow propping up your back. A good mock test score bolsters your confidence.

en: Aggressively believing that one's own group, country, or gender is superior
hook: CHAUVINISTIC: from Chauvin, a soldier who blindly worshipped Napoleon.
story: At the meeting, a manager announced, 'Women shouldn't lead engineering teams. Men simply understand machines better.' The room went silent at his chauvinistic remark. Chauvinistic means believing your own group is superior, whether that's your nation or your gender. The word comes from Nicolas Chauvin, an overly patriotic French soldier.

en: An expert judge in matters of taste, especially art, food, or drink
hook: CONNOISSEUR: 'connaître' is French for 'to know'. One who really knows.
story: Uncle Mamun is a true biryani connoisseur. One bite, and he can tell the rice type, whether the meat was marinated overnight, and which Old Dhaka shop made it. A connoisseur is an expert with refined taste, especially in art, food, music, or wine. He doesn't just enjoy; he judges with knowledge.

en: To hide one's real feelings or motives; to pretend
bn: আসল মনোভাব গোপন করা; ভান করা
hook: DIS-SEMBLE: DIS-RESEMBLE, showing a face that doesn't resemble your true feelings.
story: When the boss asked if he liked the new project, Kamal smiled and said, 'Absolutely, sir!' Inside, he hated it. He was dissembling, hiding his true feelings behind a false face. To dissemble is to conceal real motives or emotions. Don't confuse it with disassemble, which means to take apart.

en: Showing stubborn, persistent determination
hook: DOGGED: like a DOG holding a bone, refusing to let go.
story: Mitu failed the GRE twice. Instead of quitting, she studied every evening for six more months with dogged determination. On her third attempt, she scored 325. Dogged means tenaciously persistent, like a dog that won't let go of a bone. A dogged detective never drops a case.

en: To trick or deceive someone; a person who is easily fooled
hook: DUPE: a DOPE who gets fooled.
story: A caller claiming to be from the bank asked Rafi's grandfather for his card's pin number to 'fix an urgent problem.' He believed it, and lost twenty thousand taka. He had been duped. To dupe is to trick someone into believing something false. The victim of such a trick is also called a dupe.

en: Based on observation and experiment rather than theory
hook: EMPIRICAL: built on EXPERIENCE and EXPERIMENT, like an EMPIRE built brick by brick.
story: Everyone said that studying with music helps. Sara didn't trust opinions; she wanted empirical evidence. She tested herself for two weeks: one week with music, one without. Her scores were higher in silence. Empirical means based on observation and experiment, not theory. Scientists rely on empirical data.

en: To cause or give rise to a feeling or situation
hook: EN-GENDER: GENerates, GENes, birth. It gives birth to something.
story: The teacher's constant praise engendered confidence in even the shyest students. On the other hand, the new tax policy engendered anger across the country. To engender is to produce, cause, or give birth to a feeling or condition. Trust engenders loyalty; unfairness engenders resentment.

en: Believing oneself inherently deserving of special privileges
bn: নিজেকে বিশেষ সুবিধার যোগ্য মনে করে এমন; অধিকারবোধসম্পন্ন
hook: ENTITLED: acts like he holds a royal TITLE.
story: The rich student cut to the front of the canteen line and said, 'Do you know who my father is?' He expected the rules not to apply to him. Everyone found him unbearably entitled. Entitled describes someone who believes they deserve special treatment without earning it. In law, you can also be entitled to a right.

en: Holding firmly to an opinion or course of action; stubbornly persistent
hook: PERTINACIOUS: PER-TENACIOUS, tenacious through and through.
story: The journalist was pertinacious. The minister's office refused her interview twelve times, but she kept calling, kept emailing, and kept waiting outside, until finally they said yes. Pertinacious means stubbornly persistent, refusing to give up. It's like tenacious, but with an extra layer of stubbornness.

en: Too bold or forward; taking liberties without permission
hook: PRESUMPTUOUS: PRESUMES things he has no right to.
story: On his first day at the job, Arif sat in the director's chair and started suggesting changes to the whole company. His coworkers were shocked at how presumptuous he was. Presumptuous means overstepping proper limits, assuming you have rights or familiarity you haven't earned.

en: Strong moral principles; honesty and decency
hook: PROBITY: a person who passes every honesty PROBE.
story: The judge was known for her probity. In thirty years, she never accepted a gift, never favored a friend, and never hid a mistake. Even her critics trusted her honesty. Probity means complete integrity and uprightness. Public officials are expected to show probity, though many don't.

en: To increase rapidly in number; to multiply
bn: দ্রুত বিস্তার লাভ করা; বংশবৃদ্ধি করা
hook: PROLIFERATE: PRO-LIFE-rate, life multiplying fast.
story: After the monsoon, mosquitoes proliferated in every puddle, flowerpot, and drain. Dengue cases soon followed. To proliferate is to grow or multiply rapidly. Coaching centers have proliferated across Dhaka; nuclear weapons proliferation means the spread of weapons to more countries.

en: Seeming true or reasonable on the surface but actually false
hook: SPECIOUS: looks SPECIAL on the surface, but it's wrong underneath.
story: 'I studied twelve hours yesterday, so I can take today off completely,' Tanvir argued. It sounded reasonable, but it was specious; memory needs daily practice, not one-day marathons. Specious means plausible-looking but actually wrong. Specious arguments are dangerous because they fool smart people.

en: Not genuine; false or fake
hook: SPURIOUS: SPURred by lies, false.
story: The certificate looked official, with a stamp and signature. But the university confirmed it was spurious; no such student had ever graduated. Spurious means fake or not genuine. A spurious argument is based on false reasoning; spurious data come from faulty experiments.

en: Based on personal feelings or opinions rather than facts
hook: SUBJECTIVE: depends on the SUBJECT, the person judging.
story: Is Kacchi biryani better than Tehari? Rafi says yes; Mitu says no. Neither is wrong, because taste is subjective. It depends on personal preference, not measurable facts. Subjective is the opposite of objective. A judge should be objective; a food critic can be subjective.

en: To undermine the power or authority of an established system
hook: SUB-VERT: turn (vert) from below (sub), flipping the system upside down.
story: The rebels didn't attack the government directly. Instead, they subverted it quietly: spreading rumors, bribing officials, and turning soldiers against their leaders. To subvert is to undermine an established authority or system from within. Artists can also subvert expectations by breaking the usual rules.

en: Showing nervousness, fear, or lack of confidence
hook: TIMOROUS: TIMID + TERROR-ous.
story: The new student stood at the classroom door, timorous, clutching her bag. When the teacher asked her name, she whispered so softly no one heard. Timorous means nervous and easily frightened. It's a close synonym of timid. A timorous government avoids any bold decisions.

en: Full of twists and turns; excessively complex
hook: TORTUOUS: twisted like a TORTOISE's winding path. Not torturous!
story: The road to Sajek Valley is tortuous: hairpin bends, steep climbs, and endless curves. Sara got carsick within an hour. Tortuous means full of twists, whether a road or an argument. Don't confuse it with torturous, which means painful. A tortuous legal process winds endlessly, though it might also feel torturous.

en: Easy to control, manage, or influence
hook: TRACTABLE: easily pulled, like a TRACTOR pulling a cart.
story: The new puppy was surprisingly tractable. Within a week, it learned to sit, stay, and wait for food. The neighbor's dog, by contrast, ignored every command. Tractable means easily managed or controlled. A tractable problem can be solved; an intractable one is stubbornly difficult.

en: Lasting only a short time; temporary
hook: TRANSIENT: in TRANSIT, just passing through.
story: The pain of failing an exam felt overwhelming at first, but it was transient. A month later, Arif barely remembered it. Transient means temporary, passing quickly. Hotels serve a transient population of travelers. Synonyms include ephemeral, fleeting, and evanescent.

en: Present or found everywhere
hook: UBIQUITOUS: 'you BE QUITE everywhere'.
story: In Dhaka, rickshaws are ubiquitous. They crowd every street, every alley, every corner of the city at every hour. Smartphones are ubiquitous too; even rickshaw pullers use them now. Ubiquitous means seeming to be everywhere at the same time. It's one of the most common GRE words.

en: To emphasize or draw attention to
hook: UNDERSCORE: draw a line UNDER a word to highlight it.
story: The doctor underscored the importance of rest: 'Not rest when you feel like it. Rest every single day for two weeks.' The repetition made the point impossible to miss. To underscore is to emphasize, like drawing a line under important words. The rising death toll underscored the need for safer roads.

en: Willing to be bribed; corrupt
hook: VENAL: VENDING machine official: put money in, get a favor out.
story: The venal officer wouldn't sign any document without a 'speed fee' slipped under the file. Pay him, and your work moved; refuse, and it vanished for months. Venal means open to bribery. Don't confuse it with venial, which means minor and forgivable. A venal official sells his duty for money.

en: To regard with deep respect and reverence
hook: VENERATE: like VENUS, treated as a goddess.
story: In the village, everyone venerated old Master Moshai, the teacher who had taught three generations without taking a single taka for extra help. When he passed, the entire district came to his funeral. To venerate is to honor someone with deep respect, almost like worship.
